clue.text: Maybe like Hannah's buddy Mike bagging Rodin bust

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it, so the buddy-and-Mike pair holds the other letters inside

parts.note: a pal is a buddy
a mic, short for microphone, is also spelt mike

indicators.note: a thing that is bust is broken, so the letters of Rodin are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Hannah's friend Mike walks off with a broken Rodin sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a sculpture, fitting Rodin, but it signals that RODIN breaks up into INDRO. The 's in Hannah's is 'is': like Hannah is, read forwards or backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The name Hannah reads the same in both directions, so a word that behaves like it is one example of a symmetrical spelling.

clue.text: Sound wheel found beneath wheels

indicators.note: in a down answer, the wheel shape is placed under the car

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car, and an Audi is a make of car
O is round like a wheel

explanation.surface: A spare wheel is discovered under a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio refers to recorded or broadcast sound, as opposed to the picture or video.

clue.text: Better electoral system? I suggest accepting it

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so the suggestion holds the electoral initials

parts.note: I move is the formal wording for proposing a motion at a meeting
PR is proportional representation

explanation.surface: A voting reformer proposes adopting a better system for elections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better electoral system' reads as one phrase, but the definition is only 'Better', a verb; 'it' refers back to the electoral system. 'I move' is formal meeting language for a proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a verb, to better something is to make it superior, the same as to improve it.

clue.text: Particular case of embezzlement in House of Parliament

indicators.note: the outer letters go inside the parliament word

parts.note: the Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are taken

explanation.surface: A specific instance of fraud has been uncovered in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks like a legal case of fraud, but it means the outside of 'embezzlement', ET. The Dáil is the Irish lower house.
explanation.definitionFit: A detail is a single item or point, the noun sense of a particular, as in 'in every particular'.

clue.text: Love letter not saying everything

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
a missive is a letter

explanation.surface: A love letter that leaves things unsaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love letter' reads as one phrase, but it splits into O and MISSIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Omissive describes leaving things out, from omission, so it fits speech that holds things back.

clue.text: African overlooking lake in a certain peninsula

indicators.note: to overlook something is to leave it out, so the lake letter is dropped

parts.note: a Liberian is someone from Liberia in West Africa
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: An African looks out over a lake on a peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' suggests a view over water, but it means ignoring: L is left out of LIBERIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain and Portugal share the Iberian peninsula, so the adjective describes things located there.

clue.text: Get bread promptly and force a podgy male to eat seconds

parts.note: to make someone do something is to force them

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so the fat word holds the letter for seconds

parts.note: podgy means fat
a buck is a male deer or rabbit

explanation.surface: Someone tells a chubby man to have second helpings at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bread' is slang for money, so the definition means earn money quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a fast buck is an idiom for earning money quickly, often dubiously, with bread as slang for cash.

clue.text: See great works in cheap accommodation

indicators.note: works as a verb means operates or reworks, so the letters are processed into new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Tourists are told to view great works of art while staying in budget lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' looks like a noun, works of art, but it is a verb signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Steerage was the lowest-priced passenger class on a ship, near the rudder gear, so it was the cheapest berth.

clue.text: Complimentary ginger beer, drinking round? This is very cold

parts.note: complimentary means given free
ginger as a noun means liveliness or zest, which is zing

indicators.note: drinking takes something in, so the beer word holds the round letter

parts.note: a pint is a measure of beer
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A free ginger beer is offered while someone buys a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ginger beer' looks like one drink, but 'ginger' gives ZING and 'beer' gives PINT.
explanation.definitionFit: Water turns to ice at zero degrees Celsius, the temperature named by this phrase, which is very cold.

clue.text: Total bill before course gets sent back

indicators.note: the bill comes ahead of the next piece in the answer

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a bill posted up

indicators.note: being sent back means the word for the course is read in reverse

parts.note: pud, short for pudding, is the dessert course in British slang

explanation.surface: At a restaurant, the bill arrives before a dish has been returned to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' means a course of a meal, in British slang the pudding or dessert, not a path.
explanation.definitionFit: To total figures is to add them up, a phrasal-verb synonym for summing.

clue.text: Period when expecting a lot of frost in high street

indicators.note: the shortened frost word goes inside the jumbled letters
high as in intoxicated, so the letters of street are in a confused state and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: a lot of, but not all, means the frost word loses its last letter

parts.note: rime is hoar frost

explanation.surface: A time of year when plenty of frost is forecast for the town's main shopping street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high street' reads as one phrase, a British town's main shopping road, but 'high' is the anagram signal, as in intoxicated; rime is a kind of frost.
explanation.definitionFit: A pregnancy is divided into three stages of about three months each, so a woman who is expecting passes through each of them.

clue.text: Online magazines containing not a single subject

parts.note: E is the prefix for electronic, as in e-mail, meaning online

indicators.note: containing means the magazine letters hold the next piece inside

parts.note: comics are magazines of strips and cartoons
no, as in 'no one', means not a single

explanation.surface: Web comics turn out to contain not one single subject of interest.
explanation.walkthrough: E-COMICS are online magazines; NO goes in after ECO.
explanation.definitionFit: Economics is an academic discipline studied at school and university, so it counts as a subject.

clue.text: Lady from Italy together with man from France

parts.note: I is the international vehicle registration code for Italy
René is a typical French man's name

explanation.surface: An Italian woman pairs up with a Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is a woman's given name, and crosswords often define names by a word for woman such as this.

clue.text: Split in the camp of King Edward

parts.note: to be for someone is to be on their side, in their camp
K is the chess abbreviation for king
Ed is the short form of Edward

explanation.surface: A division appears among the supporters of King Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forked divides into two branches, like a fork's prongs, so it is split at one end.

clue.text: E.g., Martin Luther King back from service late

parts.note: R, from rex, is the abbreviation for king

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken
late, as in 'the late chairman', means former

explanation.surface: Martin Luther King returns from a church service late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Martin Luther King' looks like one name, but the definition stops at Luther, the German who began the Protestant Reformation; 'King' gives R.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Luther led the Protestant break with Rome in the sixteenth century, so he is an example of a religious campaigner for change.

clue.text: Succeeded leaving awful manipulative fellow

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in family trees and lists of monarchs

indicators.note: awful means dreadfully bad, so the letters of leaving are mangled and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone got out of a dreadful situation involving a scheming man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' looks like it means departing, but it is the anagram fodder for VENGALI.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali is the hypnotist in Du Maurier's novel Trilby, whose name became a byword for someone who controls another person.

clue.text: Old fighter flipping sore and gruff in speech

indicators.note: flipping over turns the word for sore back to front

parts.note: raw means sore, as raw skin

indicators.note: in speech means the word for gruff is only heard, and spelt as its sound-alike

parts.note: a gruff voice is hoarse

explanation.surface: A veteran swears about soreness in a rough voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it reverses RAW to WAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A warhorse is a veteran of many campaigns, figuratively an old soldier or politician still in the fray.

clue.text: Flatter paper's held by really elderly person

indicators.note: held by means the newspaper piece sits inside the other two words

parts.note: so, as in 'so good', means really
an OAP is an old-age pensioner
FT, the Financial Times, is a newspaper; with the 's it gives FTS

explanation.surface: An old pensioner is clutching someone's newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP, old-age pensioner, is a British term for a retired person; FT is the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-soap someone is to win them over with smooth praise, an idiomatic synonym for flattering them.

clue.text: Mandarin tests? I don't know answer!

parts.note: SATs are standard assessment tests taken by schoolchildren
um is the hesitant noise made when unsure

explanation.surface: A pupil sitting a Chinese language exam admits not knowing the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mandarin' suggests the Chinese language, apt for tests, but it is the citrus fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a kind of small, easily peeled citrus fruit belonging to the mandarin family.

clue.text: Disreputable person ordered goods

parts.note: bade, past tense of bid, means ordered
G is the abbreviation for good, and two of them make goods

explanation.surface: Someone shady put in an order for merchandise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like an anagram signal on 'goods', but it is the old past tense BADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad egg is an idiom for a rotten character, someone not to be trusted.

clue.text: Ordinary, large punches a mistake in scrap

indicators.note: to punch is to make a hole, so the two letters go into the mistake word

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: In a fight, a big ordinary fellow throws punches and blunders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrap' suggests a fight, fitting the punches, but here it is the verb to discard.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrap a rule or plan is to get rid of it completely, which is to do away with it formally.

clue.text: One cuts piece of jewellery, ring that's flat

indicators.note: cuts means slices into, so the numeral goes between the jewellery and the ring

parts.note: a stud is an earring or similar small ornament
O is ring-shaped
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A jeweller trims an earring, and the ring's surface is left level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like an adjective describing the ring, but it is the noun for an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio is a one-room apartment, and in British English an apartment is called a flat.

clue.text: Youthful rogue screens old mockumentary film

indicators.note: to screen is to shield or hide, so the rogue word encloses the next letter

parts.note: a brat is a badly behaved child

explanation.surface: A young troublemaker shows an old fake documentary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screens' sounds like showing a film, apt for the subject, but here it means hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: Borat is the 2006 Sacha Baron Cohen comedy shot as a spoof documentary about a Kazakh reporter.

clue.text: Something delicate in stew? Partook regularly

parts.note: a hotpot is a meat and potato stew, as in Lancashire hotpot

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the following word

parts.note: the word whose alternate letters are picked

explanation.surface: Someone ate stew at intervals and found a dainty morsel in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A hotpot is a stew from northern England. The even letters of Partook give ATO.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot potato is an issue too sensitive to handle comfortably, an idiom for a touchy matter.

clue.text: Accountants are up and down, investing right capital

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, so the accountants enclose the right letter
in a down answer the accountants' letters read upward then downward, the same both ways

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant; written up then down it gives ACCA

explanation.surface: Accountants' fortunes rise and fall while investing in the right capital assets.
explanation.walkthrough: CA, chartered accountant, is read up (AC) then down (CA), and R goes in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital city of Ghana in West Africa.

clue.text: In Spain, what stops revolutionaries having many ups and downs

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the Spanish word sits inside the revolutionaries

parts.note: Che Guevara and a Red, a communist, are two revolutionaries
qué is Spanish for what

explanation.surface: In Spain, something halts the rebels, whose fortunes keep rising and falling.
explanation.walkthrough: Two revolutionaries are joined: Che Guevara and a Red, a communist; the Spanish word plugs the gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A chequered history or career is one marked by mixed fortunes, alternating good and bad spells.

clue.text: Ancient civilisation's preserved?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, an adjective: belonging to the Inca people of Peru
second meaning, read as two words: kept in a tin, as preserved food is

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading, where the word splits two and three.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca empire flourished in the Andes before the Spanish conquest, and the adjective refers to its people and culture.

clue.text: Woke up and reached crisis point

parts.note: to come to is to regain consciousness, so came to means woke
a team that is up is ahead, leading

explanation.surface: Someone woke and things suddenly got critical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woke up' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'Woke' gives the first two words and 'up' the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: A boil or a dispute comes to a head when it reaches its peak and must burst or be resolved.
